articles.title: Ping64|Why PDF and Word Files Can Hide Different Kinds of Trouble Inside
articles.excerpt: A colleague sends you two files: a report saved as a PDF and the same report saved as a Word document. Both look harmless, both open fine, yet security teams treat them quite differently. The question…
articles.body: A colleague sends you two files: a report saved as a PDF and the same report saved as a Word document. Both look harmless, both open fine, yet security teams treat them quite differently. The question of which format is more likely to carry something bad has no simple answer, because each format hides risk in different places. Understanding those differences can help you make smarter choices about which attachments you open and how you open them. Simple analogy A PDF is a bit like a printed photograph of a page. Most of what you see is frozen in place, and the file simply describes how the page should look. A Word document is more like a workshop with machines still plugged in.
articles.author: Cyrus

articles.title: Matching Nickel Alloy Names, UNS Numbers and ASTM Specs in Python
articles.excerpt: If you have ever cleaned up a parts list for a process plant, you know the problem. One line says "Inconel 625", the next says "Alloy 625", a drawing says "UNS N06625", and a European supplier writes…
articles.body: If you have ever cleaned up a parts list for a process plant, you know the problem. One line says "Inconel 625", the next says "Alloy 625", a drawing says "UNS N06625", and a European supplier writes "2.4856". All four mean the same material, but a plain string match treats them as four different things. This post builds a small Python lookup that maps those names to one record. It is a good exercise in normalizing messy input, and the same pattern works for any catalog with aliases. The data Each alloy gets one record keyed by its UNS number. The record holds the common names, the EN material number, and the ASTM product specification for each form.

articles.title: The continuation cell a DOCX vertical merge leaves behind still owns a grid column
articles.excerpt: A vertical merge in Word hides the rows it swallows on screen only. Inside the file every one of those rows still carries a cell of its own: a real , with a bare in its properties and an empty paragra…
articles.body: A vertical merge in Word hides the rows it swallows on screen only. Inside the file every one of those rows still carries a cell of its own: a real <w:tc> , with a bare <w:vMerge/> in its properties and an empty paragraph for a body, sitting below the cell that carries <w:vMerge w:val="restart"/> and opens the group. Nothing in the file marks the continuation as gone. It sits in its row, it keeps its place in the table grid, and it is the one cell a converter has to decide not to emit. The numbers below come from one pass over one self-made sample, so they describe this document rather than ranking anything. The file is 43,790 bytes, built on purpose with three tables: one merging across, one merging down, and a mixed one at 5 columns by 4 rows.
articles.author: yue xing

articles.title: Why our AI asks "which metric?" before drawing a chart
articles.excerpt: A small design decision we keep coming back to: when a request is ambiguous, PowerDataChat asks a clarifying question instead of guessing. Example: "Chart revenue and margin by month." Revenue is in c…
articles.body: A small design decision we keep coming back to: when a request is ambiguous, PowerDataChat asks a clarifying question instead of guessing. Example: "Chart revenue and margin by month." Revenue is in currency, margin is a percentage. Put both on one chart and it becomes hard to read. So instead of picking for you, it asks which metric you want, or how you want them shown. Three related behaviours follow the same idea: Starter questions. An empty chat box is intimidating. After a file is connected, the AI suggests questions based on that file, so a new user has somewhere to start. Honest "missing data" answers. If you ask about a column that does not exist, it says what is missing and suggests alternatives instead of inventing values. Follow-ups keep context.

articles.body: Last Saturday my neighbor knocked and asked if I could look at her Wi-Fi, because it had been dropping for weeks and the ISP hotline kept telling her to reboot the box. I figured it would take twenty minutes. It took most of the afternoon, and honestly it was more satisfying than half of my work week. For context, I spend my weekdays on network and security work, so people assume I can fix a home router in my sleep. I usually can, but home networks are their own special zoo. Consumer gear makes brave choices on your behalf, hides every setting behind a companion app, and never tells you what it assumed. What I actually found Her setup was a small museum of good intentions.

articles.title: 5 UCP and Schema.org Failures Blocking AI Shopping Agents from Your Store
articles.excerpt: What we found scanning real e-commerce sites for Universal Commerce Protocol readiness, and how to fix each one AI shopping agents are arriving. Google and Shopify introduced the Universal Commerce Pr…
articles.body: What we found scanning real e-commerce sites for Universal Commerce Protocol readiness, and how to fix each one AI shopping agents are arriving. Google and Shopify introduced the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) at Google I/O. Zalando, DoorDash, and Walmart have announced agent-driven checkout. But when you drop to the technical layer, most stores are invisible to these agents. I built Karuma ( https://karuma.dev/en ) to measure exactly that. It is a free, no-registration scanner that streams a live NDJSON audit of any public storefront against the UCP specification. It checks three layers: Layer 1 ( /.well-known/ucp manifest) : valid JSON (not HTML, not a soft-404), declared capabilities, version YYYY-MM-DD , HTTPS, and working transport ( REST , MCP , A2A , Embedded ).

articles.body: In 1964, Italian director Sergio Leone redefined the Western movie genre with A Fistful of Dollars . Eschewing the relatively simplistic morality tales of earlier films, Leone’s protagonist wasn’t a noble hero, but an opportunistic gunslinger who pits two rival Old West gangs against each other to score a big payday. Despite the moral complexity of it all — or, more likely, because of it — A Fistful of Dollars was an international success that proved three things: audiences were ready for a new kind of Western, America no longer had a monopoly on the genre, and Clint Eastwood was a bankable movie star.

articles.body: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627. Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast. A Falcon 9 first stage rests on a SpaceX drone ship shortly after launching the USSF-627 mission on Nov. 11, 2026. articles.title: NASA kick-starts a fresh push to bring Mars samples home
articles.excerpt: NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for Mars Sample Return (MSR), called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture.
articles.body: A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet. NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth. The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).

articles.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
articles.excerpt: Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.
articles.body: Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound. Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star. Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space.
